items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: The interviewee discusses Marshall Stearns in the context of a letter he received and his views on jazz history, but does not describe a personal meeting or direct professional collaboration, only a correspondence/argument.

ctx.x: You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They…

The letter here from... Let me see. I'll give you the full letterhead. It's a letter from Marshall W. Stearns. Yale Hot Club, 6th Linwood Place, New Haven, Connecticut. M. W. Stearns, President. Charter Unit of the UHCA. January the 11th, 1937, Mr. D.J. La Rocca, Earl Theater, Washington, D.C. Dear Nick, I have all your records from Liberty Stable Blues to the recent disc. I like the earlier ones better. Between you and me, our last argument should furnish you with plenty of publicity. I do think, however, that…

From this article, many other articles was copied. This is a work, you've got to be either pro-communist or a communist to work this way. There's a letter to keep me quiet. I'm a working man, trying to support a family. This man has not stopped writing about Negroes, yet he knows different. Now here's Brown's letter. To show you Brown was lying, I want to show you, I want to have him read this in there, what the name of his band was, in case you ever read Downbeat on 1936, and see what they have did to a man who…
